source.title: Scaling and context steer LLMs along the same computational path as the human brain
source.authors: Jos'ephine Raugel; Jérémy Rapin; Stéphane d'Ascoli; Valentin Wyart; Jean-R'emi King

record.tranche_reason: The study measures correspondence between LLM representations and human brain responses, not representational convergence between AI models or the other behaviors specified in V1–V7. Its results concern a related biological–artificial comparison, so they do not test a listed version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports brain–LLM alignment and temporal-order results, including scaling and context trends. These are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the listed model-to-model convergence versions. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures alignment between LLM layer activations and human MEG responses: a ridge map from brain to LLM activations, plus the order in which layers peak over time. It never compares representations between AI models, vision–language pairs, seeds, features or similarity metrics. The brain is not an independently trained model in the sense V1–V7 name, so this is a related construct. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis is cited only once, in the discussion, as one possible explanation. No version is tested; the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct: LLM layer order mirrors the order of MEG brain responses. This alignment holds across transformers and SSMs, needs pretraining and causal processing, and grows with model size and context length, logarithmically and with saturation around 70B. Word predictability alone does not explain it. Whether size and context act directly or through confounds such as linguistic performance remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits a ridge-regression mapping from MEG activity to LLM activations and measures held-out prediction and temporal ordering. It does not compare pairwise representational distances between independently trained models, as the claim's cited sources do.
record.method_sensitivity: Brain–LLM temporal and representational scores vary with model size and context length. Bidirectional models have substantially lower, non-significant temporal scores than causal LLMs. Word predictability did not significantly affect temporal score in the tested comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain–LLM representational and temporal alignment rise logarithmically with Pythia model size (temporal vs log size r = 0.87) and with context length (Llama-3.2 3B). The authors report a plateau, with Llama 3.3 70B showing no major gain over 3B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM–brain (MEG) alignment, including the temporal ordering of layer computations, increases with model size and context length, with diminishing returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Temporal brain alignment appears across transformers and state-space models, is absent in unpretrained models, and is low and non-significant for bidirectional models whose representational alignment is comparable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The layer-order correspondence between LLMs and the brain is architecture-general among causal pretrained models but depends on causality and training.

fits_no_version.finding: Temporal score correlates with top-3 next-token accuracy across context lengths (r = 0.77) but not across Pythia sizes (r = 0.2). Temporal and representational brain scores correlate with each other (r = 0.54).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capability explains brain–LLM temporal alignment only in some conditions; representational and temporal brain alignment covary.

record.problems: The paper's evidence concerns brain–LLM alignment rather than AI model-to-model representational convergence. The main MEG dataset has only 3 participants; the authors note that between-individual variation remains unknown. The authors also state that context and model-size effects may be confounded by uncontrolled variables such as linguistic performance. Some appendix findings are described without numerical scores in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant brain–LLM results were left out; figure-only values not described numerically in the text were not transcribed.

untested.parts: No model-to-model alignment is measured as size or capability varies; only brain–LLM alignment versus size.
No comparison of seeds or initializations.
No mapping between models; the linear map is from MEG to LLM activations.
No variation of the similarity metric or neighbour count for model-to-model similarity.
The plateau and partial convergence concern brain–LLM alignment, not model-to-model alignment; shared data or objectives as a cause are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Not recorded, and not tied to any version: GPT2-XL temporal score r = 0.85; predictability quartiles (r = 0.92 most expected, r = 0.83 most surprising, difference p = 0.61); Mixtral-8x7B results. Only 3 MEG subjects. The 'partial convergence' language refers to brains and LLMs, not to models with each other.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure alignment between independently trained AI models, or compare their representational distances as model size and capability vary.
No paired image-caption vision–language model alignment is measured.
The paper does not compare same-architecture networks trained from different initializations or assess shared features or subspaces.
The linear map predicts LLM activations from brain activity; it does not test mapping one model's representations to another's, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
The paper does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
The study varies context and word selection for brain–LLM alignment, but does not test metric, neighbor-count, or input-distribution dependence of model-to-model convergence.
The paper reports partial brain–LLM correspondence and possible plateaus, but does not determine whether shared AI training data or objectives explain model-to-model alignment.
